items.title: “One War at a Time”: President Abraham Lincoln and the 1861 Trent Affair
items.summary: A diplomatic crisis 165 years ago between the United States and Britain over two captured Confederate envoys nearly triggered a third Anglo-American war.

ai.sum: CFR historical piece recalls the 1861 Trent Affair, a US-Britain diplomatic crisis over two captured Confederate envoys.

brief.summary: The authors, writing for the Council on Foreign Relations, recount the 1861 Trent affair, when Union naval captain Charles Wilkes seized Confederate envoys Mason and Slidell from a British mail steamer, nearly provoking an Anglo-American war. They argue that the crisis was defused less by legal merit than by Lincoln's strategic restraint, Prince Albert's softening of London's rhetoric, and the passage of time. Lincoln concluded that the Union could fight only one war at a time, so the envoys were released, and Seward framed the release in a way that rested on the neutral-trade principles Britain had long resisted. The piece presents this as a lesson that the conflicts a leader avoids can matter as much as those they wage. It is a historical essay by James M. Lindsay, republished to mark the US 250th anniversary.
brief.argument: Lincoln's decision to avoid a war with Britain over the Trent seizure, accepting the envoys' release to focus on the Confederacy, was a strategic choice that helped the Union win the Civil War.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the 2026 US midterm results, which produced divided government, do not clearly show a mandate for Democrats. Drawing on a sociological reading, they contend that rejection of an incumbent does not imply confidence in the alternative, so voters may punish Republicans without endorsing Democratic policy. They trace a pattern since 2016 in which negative voting, motivated by fear of the opponent, has mobilised voters more effectively than loyalty to a programme. This dynamic weakens parties' incentives to respond to internal criticism and risks mistaking electoral victory for approval of every policy. The piece also warns that when trust in elections depends on which candidate wins, institutions lose their standing as a shared referee. Accepting a legitimate winner's right to govern, they argue, must be separated from disagreement with that winner's intentions.
brief.argument: Divided government after the 2026 midterms reflects negative voting against Trump and the Republicans rather than a mandate for the Democratic programme, and the resulting trust in elections has become conditional on who wins.
recommendations: Parties should not treat electoral victory as endorsement of their full agenda
Distinguish challenges to electoral legitimacy from scrutiny of a government's policies

ai.sum: Atlantic Council argues Putin is using peace talks, including a planned US-Ukraine-Russia summit in Abu Dhabi, to buy time rather than end the war.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Russian President Putin's goal in Ukraine is effective political control, pursued mainly by undermining Western, especially American, support for Kyiv. They say Trump has offered at least six proposals since spring 2025, which Zelenskyy accepted and Putin rejected or deflected, and that recent US steps (resuming Russian diesel shipments, waiving sanctions in the Graham bill, cutting Starlink intelligence to Ukraine, and entertaining a Putin-Xi summit) have eased Moscow's position. Putin's only concession is a procedural working-level meeting in Abu Dhabi, led by Vladimir Medinsky, whose terms remain unchanged. The authors also argue that Moscow's demand that former Warsaw Pact and Baltic states leave NATO shows the Kremlin still refuses serious negotiation, so expectations for the talks should be very modest.
brief.argument: Putin is using talks to keep Washington distanced from Ukraine rather than to reach a stable peace, and US concessions have strengthened rather than constrained him.
recommendations: Pressure the side that rejects reasonable proposals, as Trump has said he would
Stop unilateral concessions to Moscow such as sanctions waivers and intelligence cutoffs to Ukraine
Keep NATO in the security role of any European settlement
brief.turkey: Türkiye's mediation and Black Sea interests depend on whether Abu Dhabi produces real movement, and the authors' view that talks are procedural suggests Ankara should not expect a breakthrough.

items.title: The six strategic mistakes that led to US defeat in Afghanistan
items.summary: Twenty-five years on, the United States' defeat in Afghanistan appears less inevitable than the result of decisions that undermined its ability to prevent the Taliban's resurgence. The post The six strategic mistakes that led to US defeat in Afghanistan appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: An Atlantic Council analysis argues the US defeat in Afghanistan resulted from six strategic mistakes rather than inevitability.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the US defeat in Afghanistan resulted from six discrete strategic choices rather than from the conflict being unwinnable. They say Washington tried to build a centralised Afghan state with a national army and Kabul supremacy, backing Hamid Karzai, which ran against the country's history as a loose confederation and fed Taliban propaganda about corruption. They add that the Bush administration's distraction with Iraq left the early Taliban resurgence unaddressed, and that Washington never pressed Pakistan hard enough over its sanctuaries and support for the Taliban and Haqqani network. The surge into Marjah and Helmand, rather than securing Kabul and Kandahar, squandered momentum, and firing McChrystal weakened it further. Finally, they argue the US missed a cheaper option in 2017: using money and contractors to rent the loyalty of regional power-brokers, as Najibullah had done.
brief.argument: The US lost in Afghanistan because of six avoidable strategic choices, chiefly the attempt to build a centralised state and the failure to pressure Pakistan, rather than because the war was unwinnable.
recommendations: Change as little as necessary: work with existing local power structures rather than imposing a centralised national model
Match force posture to the political goals set, rather than pursuing a light footprint alongside ambitious nation-building
Secure the population centres first and farm out outlying provinces to local allies at minimum cost
Use sustained, credible pressure on sanctuary states such as Pakistan, backed by willingness to act against them
brief.turkey: The lessons on imposing a centralised model on a fragmented polity and on the limits of pressuring a neighbouring state that hosts armed groups may bear on Türkiye's approach to Syria and its Syrian Kurdish and PKK-linked files.

ai.sum: Atlantic Council argues any Ukraine peace deal must set a date for Kyiv's EU accession and that Washington can help Brussels overcome obstacles.

brief.summary: The authors argue that a lasting end to Russia's war on Ukraine should include a credible path to Ukraine's EU membership, since leaving Ukraine in a neutral gray zone would invite future Russian pressure. They note that the Trump administration's own peace plans already mention EU membership, but that the accession process is stalled by member-state vetoes, budget worries and farmers' anger over competition. They propose a US-Europe-Ukraine 'grand bargain': Washington would press Kyiv on EU-required reforms, give Europe a larger seat in peace talks, and offer financing, agricultural market arrangements and investment support in exchange for advantageous commercial and security terms. They present this as serving US economic and burden-sharing interests while acknowledging that enlargement remains an EU decision.
brief.argument: Ukraine's EU membership should be a core element of a durable settlement, and Washington can help unlock it through a conditional grand bargain with Europe and Kyiv.
recommendations: Involve European leaders and key member states directly in peace talks to generate buy-in for Ukraine's EU path.
Coordinate with the EU on the reforms Washington will back and press Kyiv for firmer commitments on rule-of-law and anti-corruption.
Offer agricultural arrangements, such as price floors or purchase guarantees for Ukrainian products sold outside the EU, to ease member-state concerns.
Condition US loans or grants to Ukraine on completing EU-specified reforms.

brief.summary: The author argues that foreign policy mattered in the 2026 midterms because voters linked it directly to affordability, citing the Iran war and tariffs as drivers of higher costs. Drawing on CFR polling and commentary from figures such as Jessica Huseman and JD Vance, the piece contends that voters judge foreign policy by its domestic consequences. It predicts continuity in executive-led policy, since Congress has limited ability to constrain the president on tariffs or Iran except through must-pass legislation. The author suggests a narrower, more strategic tariff approach could address affordability concerns, and notes that Democratic statehouse wins and local referenda against data centres signal political resistance to AI infrastructure expansion. The piece closes by stressing the uncertainty of prediction markets.
brief.argument: Affordability concerns linked to the Iran war and tariffs made foreign policy decisive in the midterms, and the president is likely to continue his executive-driven course because Congress can do little to constrain him.

brief.argument: The midterms were a rebuke of Trump's broken promises rather than a shift to a coherent Democratic ideology, and the post-Trump succession on both sides remains unsettled.

brief.argument: Golden Dome cannot provide effective protection against long-range ballistic missiles, and pursuing it would increase nuclear risk by provoking adversary buildups, countermeasures and faster, more mistake-prone crises.
recommendations: Recognise that any deployed strategic missile defence has only limited capability against even a small number of missiles, to avoid hair-trigger postures.

Avoid deploying boost-phase intercept systems that would require pre-delegated launch authority and automated threat assessment.

brief.summary: The author argues that EU capability coalitions are the right direction but face an accountability gap: European defence capacity is fragmented across national ministries, ports, railways, power grids, telecoms and private firms, and no institution owns the complete system. Rather than waiting for a single federal structure, he proposes starting with a few willing countries and a limited set of capabilities such as military mobility, logistics, air and missile defence, and surveillance. For each capability, a lead integrator (not a super-owner) would map the delivery chain, expose dependencies, monitor readiness and answer for whether the outcome can be produced. He suggests a 'Defence Capacity Statement' as a common discipline: required effect, usable capacity, critical dependencies, accountable owners and evidence. The Nordic and Baltic states are offered as a natural test case. The core message is outcome first, then visibility, control and accountability, with finance following capacity requirements.
brief.argument: Europe's fragmented defence capacity needs a designated lead integrator accountable for whether each agreed capability actually delivers its required outcome, rather than more coordination or a single common owner.
recommendations: Start with a small group of willing countries and a limited number of capabilities such as military mobility, logistics, air and missile defence, surveillance and energy resilience.

They stress that wars can begin without leaders choosing them, as escalation logic overrides prudent planning. Their central lesson is that policymakers must understand past mistakes and end small conflicts before they grow into something far larger. They also note that information moves faster and artificial intelligence increasingly places some decisions beyond human control, making the lesson more urgent. brief.argument: Great power war is a rising risk because today's multipolar, nationalist world resembles the pre-1914 system, and leaders can be pushed into escalation they do not want, so small conflicts must be ended early.

brief.summary: The authors, nine CFR experts, assess how a Democratic-controlled Congress alongside a Republican White House could shape U.S. foreign policy. They argue that Congress's main levers are spending, oversight, Senate confirmations and sanctions, but that the lack of a veto-proof majority limits what Democrats can reverse. Expected priorities include affordability, hearings on the Iran war, scrutiny of Gulf investment and Israel aid, and the rebuilding of foreign aid capacity. On tariffs, Ukraine and AI, the experts see presidential control and bipartisan limits as the constraint. They also note that the Iran war and cost of living influenced voters, and that Asian partners hope for restraint on tariffs.
brief.argument: A Democratic Congress will mainly use oversight, spending and confirmations to challenge the Trump administration's foreign policy, but without a veto-proof majority it cannot reverse core policies such as tariffs or the Ukraine approach.
recommendations: Use appropriations and oversight to constrain Middle East policy and hold the administration to account on the Iran war
Rebuild foreign assistance and diplomatic tools that the administration weakened
Pursue bipartisan legislation on AI safety reporting and incident disclosure before broader standards
Secure Republican support on defence and Europe, such as troop-level baselines in Europe

ai.sum: Hudson Institute published its Ukraine military situation report for November 4, 2026, featuring a commentary by Can Kasapoğlu.

brief.summary: The authors describe a Russian air campaign in October 2026 at unprecedented scale, with thousands of drones and around 150 ballistic missiles fired at Ukraine, and they highlight the new Dan-T jet-powered loitering munition as a cheaper, flexible strike option aimed at overwhelming Ukrainian air defences. They report heavy strikes on energy infrastructure ahead of winter and say Russia suffered its worst month of personnel losses, while Ukraine made a small net territorial gain. On air defence, they argue that a newly approved $2.1 billion US sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 interceptors cannot meet Ukraine's urgent needs because deliveries are years away, so Kyiv is pursuing faster options such as drawing on existing US stocks or European transfers. They also flag protests over conscription near Kyiv as a possible vector for Russian exploitation of domestic instability, though they say Moscow's involvement is unverified.
brief.argument: Russia's mass drone and missile campaign is outpacing Ukraine's air defence, and the Patriot deal does not solve the near-term shortfall.
recommendations: Kyiv should press Washington to release interceptors from existing US inventories and replenish them later with new production.
Kyiv should seek to move ahead of other customers in Lockheed Martin's Patriot production queue.
European allies should transfer Patriot interceptors from their own arsenals in exchange for replacement missiles after 2030.
Ukraine should introduce conscription reforms to limit Russia's ability to exploit domestic grievances.

items.title: The midterms are done. Time for the fiscal clashes to begin.
items.summary: The Democrats’ victory in the 2026 US midterm elections sets the stage for major showdowns on the federal budget and the debt ceiling. The post The midterms are done. Time for the fiscal clashes to begin. appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Democrats' victory in the 2026 US midterms sets up major federal budget and debt ceiling showdowns, according to Atlantic Council analysis.

brief.summary: The authors argue that after the midterms, US fiscal fights over the debt ceiling and federal budget will intensify, with a debt limit of $41.1 trillion projected to be breached in the first half of next year, prompting extraordinary Treasury measures by spring. They contend this clash is unusual because Democrats hold strong majorities in both chambers and global investors already doubt US debt credibility, with the ten-year yield crossing 5 percent in September. They note the US is almost alone in using a fixed debt cap rather than one pegged to growth, which they say preserves Congressional leverage. They suggest the lame-duck session could extend the debt ceiling and fund the government, though a budget standoff with the White House seems unavoidable as the presidential cycle heats up, with global economic consequences.
brief.argument: Partisan fiscal showdowns over the debt ceiling and budget after the midterms could threaten US creditworthiness and rattle the global economy.
recommendations: Extend the debt ceiling during the lame-duck session to take it off the table for the new Congress
Replace the fixed debt limit with a cap pegged to growth, such as a debt-to-GDP ratio, as most other countries do
Pass a bipartisan hybrid spending package in the lame duck that funds selected agencies for the full fiscal year

ai.sum: German federal politicians welcomed the Democrats' midterm win while warning that Trump remains unpredictable; the AfD diverged.

brief.summary: The piece is a news roundup of German political reactions to the 2026 US midterm results, in which Democrats won majorities in both chambers of Congress. It gathers statements from parties across the spectrum: CDU's Jürgen Hardt reads the result as a verdict on Trump's foreign policy and notes the contradiction between Trump's stated aversion to military conflict and his actual use of force, including in Iran. SPD and Green figures stress that Trump remains unpredictable, so Europe must strengthen its own security. Defence minister Pistorius and NATO's Whitaker stress the stability of military ties and the continued validity of Article 5. The AfD sees Trump as still the decisive authority on foreign policy, and the Left links the vote to cost-of-living grievances. The article presents these as German reactions rather than an analytical verdict.
brief.argument: German political reactions to the Democratic midterm win are divided, with most expecting Trump to remain unpredictable in foreign policy, even as military cooperation with the US stays stable.
recommendations: Strengthen European security policy and defence capacity independently of the US

items.title: The G.I. and the Paperback: A World War II Love Story
items.summary: On June 5, 1944, as soldiers lined British shores, preparing for their perilous journey to the beaches of Normandy, Special Services units handed out comfort items, from packs of cigarettes to candy. But one item was more sought after than any other: books. Crouched on the crowded decks awaiting Eisenhower’s call to launch, the men clasped their standard-issue rifles and clutched their standard-issue paperbacks. They were armed with stories: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn,…

ai.sum: A historical account describes how paperback books were prized by US soldiers preparing for the Normandy landings in June 1944.

brief.summary: The author recounts how the Council on Books in Wartime, a group of civilian publishing figures, partnered with the US Army and Navy to produce Armed Services Editions: pocket-sized paperbacks distributed to servicemembers in World War II. The authors' lens is that the books met a niche need quickly and cheaply, with royalties set at one cent per copy. The piece argues that many servicemembers first read literature cover to cover through these books, which fed postwar growth in college attendance under the G.I. Bill and a paperback publishing boom. It concludes that today's defense planning, increasingly technical, might also benefit from simple, humane solutions delivered with civilian partners.
brief.argument: Simple, humane gifts delivered through civilian-military partnership can have lasting effects on servicemembers and society, as the Armed Services Editions did in World War II.
recommendations: Look for simple solutions to unmet servicemember needs that civilian partners can help deliver
Recognise that servicemembers' human needs for leisure and escape matter alongside technical capability

brief.summary: The authors argue that Jordan's airstrikes in southern Syria, which killed 10 people on 26 October, exposed the fragility of the Jordan-Syria rapprochement. Jordan says it coordinated the strikes and killed over 20 Islamic State members; Damascus says it had no advance notice, reports no IS casualties, and calls the strikes a sovereignty violation. The piece presents this as a test of Syria's 'zero problems' policy: diplomatic warming without effective security cooperation leaves cross-border threats likely to recur as diplomatic crises. Both governments have publicly chosen restraint and agreed a joint committee on the strikes, but the authors stress that the question of why Jordan bypassed Damascus remains unanswered and that the two states need to define mutual responsibilities and build a security partnership.
brief.argument: Without an effective security partnership, Jordan-Syria rapprochement remains fragile and cross-border threats risk becoming recurring diplomatic crises.
recommendations: Define mutual responsibilities on cross-border security between Damascus and Amman.
Build a security partnership capable of protecting people on both sides of the border.
Use the joint investigation committee to resolve disputes over intelligence and coordination.

The authors describe it as a move to secure Sonatrach's Kafra oilfield investments and the planned Trans-Saharan gas pipeline, and to safeguard Algeria's southern hinterland. They argue the venture faces serious risks: armed groups such as ISGS and Boko Haram cells exploiting the Salvador Triangle smuggling corridor, insurgent attacks on energy infrastructure, and cheap drones changing tactics. They also warn of friction with other outside powers in the Sahel, including Russia, Türkiye, Morocco and France, and conclude that Algeria's ability to protect its investments depends more on managing a multi-actor competition than on conventional military strength.
brief.argument: Algeria's Niger deployment is driven by energy-investment protection and border security, but it carries serious operational risks from non-state armed groups using drones and from competing foreign powers in the Sahel.
recommendations: Algiers should keep coordination channels open with Russia and Türkiye to avoid misunderstandings on the ground.

items.title: Who Polices the Blockchain? The Binance Heist and the New Gatekeepers
items.summary: The institutions that have the authority to police international finance are no longer necessarily the institutions that possess the capabilities to do so.

ai.sum: RUSI analysis argues that institutions with policing authority over finance no longer necessarily have the capabilities to police crypto flows after the Binance case.

brief.summary: The author argues that the US$6.3 billion Binance heist, attributed in the piece to North Korean hackers, exposes a shift in who holds operational control over financial security. Criminals exploit digital finance, borders and speed, while governments keep legal authority but increasingly depend on private firms: stablecoin issuers that froze US$2.4 billion and blockchain analytics firms that tracked funds in near real time. The piece warns that this creates tension between legal authority and operational capability, and questions whether the FATF's government-centred standards are keeping pace. It concludes that freezing assets is not recovering them, and that the real test is how much illicit value is denied to its users.
brief.argument: Governments retain legal authority over financial security but now depend on private companies with superior operational capability, and the existing standard-setting model, led by the FATF, has not adapted to this shift.
recommendations: Set clear expectations on when private firms may unilaterally freeze assets, share information or intervene in transactions, with appropriate safeguards.
Connect private capabilities to public authorities so law enforcement and regulators can act at digital speed while preserving due process.
Radically re-examine the model on which the response to financial crime is built, since decades of standards have not kept up with the threat.

items.title: Is 2026 the New 1914?
items.summary: We Discuss: Mentioned on the Episode: Norman Angell, The Great Illusion, Simpkin, Marshall, Hamilton, Kent & Co. Odd Arne Westad, The Coming Storm: Power, Conflict, and Warnings from History, Allen Lane Odd Arne Westad, “Trump, Xi, and the Specter of 1914,” Foreign Affairs

ai.sum: A CFR podcast episode draws parallels between 2026 and 1914, citing Odd Arne Westad's warnings about US-China tensions.

brief.summary: The authors, in this CFR podcast with historian Odd Arne Westad, argue that today's multipolar, post-globalization world resembles the period before 1914 more than the Cold War or the 1930s. Westad holds that the economic gains of globalization have turned the countries that benefited most against it, as rising powers catch up, and that nationalism, populism and international terrorism have grown alongside. He stresses that World War I was not inevitable: leaders had many communication channels but lacked the willingness to play for time and did not understand each other's core strategic interests. Westad rejects the view that economic interdependence or nuclear weapons will reliably prevent great-power war, pointing to the 1914 precedent in which trade ties did not stop the war and to new weapons and proliferation that he considers unsettling. He also cautions that historical analogies carry real weight in policymaking and must be chosen and used with care.
brief.argument: Westad argues that the world of the 2020s resembles the pre-1914 era of globalization, rising powers and mutual misunderstanding, and that interdependence and nuclear deterrence are not reliable safeguards against great-power war.
recommendations: Use historical analogies with humility and accuracy, since policymakers reach for them under pressure.
Work to understand the core strategic interests of rival powers, not only to keep talking to them.
Do not assume economic interdependence will by itself deter war.

ai.sum: CFR podcast discusses the US economic fallout from the midterm elections and cost-of-living pressures voters prioritise.

brief.summary: The authors, host Rebecca Patterson and KPMG chief economist Diane Swonk, read the midterm results as voter frustration with inflation, health-care costs and stagnant wages, and see a mandate for Congress to focus on cost of living and affordability. They point to household debt strain, with about 20 percent of households behind on debt payments, and blame data center construction for pushing up electricity and water costs and wages in skilled trades. On the labour market they describe a 'low hire, low fire' economy with low turnover, and they note that real wages have lagged inflation for 13 straight months. They argue inflation is concentrated in food, energy and health care and that shocks have become endemic rather than episodic. Swonk argues the Fed should be more decisive, forecasting at least two rate hikes by early next year, and rejects the view that inflation near 3 percent is acceptable.
brief.argument: The authors argue that voters have signalled that cost-of-living pressures are their top priority and that the Fed should tighten decisively because inflation shocks have become persistent.
recommendations: Congress should focus on cost of living and affordability.
The Fed should raise rates, with at least two hikes by early next year.
Financial literacy should be expanded because it narrows the opportunity gap and strengthens the economy.
